agent_notes: yechidati: lit. 'my only one'. All five English versions soften it ('darling', 'life', 'only one'). Commentators in the packet read it as the soul that is one and unique (Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion). I kept 'my only one' in the literal layer and 'my one life' in the dramatic.

The shift from the imperative 'save me' to the perfect 'you have answered me' is the hinge of the psalm. Hebrew has no change of tense marker here; I kept a plain perfect in the literal layer. agent_notes: Reviewer request: the earlier English said 'the nations slain by Israel'. Radak (the second reading he gives, in his father's name) says the 'descenders to dust' are those who killed Israel, who are in Gehenna, and God will not give life to any of them (citing Joel 4:21 and Isaiah 60:17). The commentary now gives the killers, not the slain, attributed to Radak. The Hebrew itself names no nation and no Israel, so the literal and dramatic layers keep the text's own words.

The verse is a famous crux and the five English versions split. KJV, ASV and Webster read the first clause as future ('shall eat and worship'); YLT keeps the Hebrew perfect ('have eaten'). BBE turns the last clause into 'has not enough for the life of his soul'. The last clause, 'ונפשו לא חיה', has a third-person singular verb with a 'his' that has no antecedent in the plural clause before it; I kept 'his' and 'he' literally. I did not adopt any emendation of the consonants.
